Part 1

Build a Strong Self-Introduction

Learn → Observe → Check → Apply

Step 1 • Learn

Principles for Writing a Self-Introduction

Recommended Time

2–3 minutes

Recommended Length

200–300 English words

1. Keep it relevant

Select information that helps demonstrate your fit for the opportunity.

2. Follow a clear structure

Organize your introduction logically rather than listing information.

3. Support strengths with evidence

Connect strengths with relevant experience or achievements.

4. Be concise and natural

Prioritize important information and avoid memorizing every sentence word-for-word.

Recommended Structure

① Personal Information

Degree
Location
Current position
Professional background

② Relevant Experience

Work experience
International experience
Achievements

③ Strengths

Skills
Competencies
Evidence

④ Motivation

Why this role?
Why this company?
Career connection

Part 1 Key Takeaway

A strong self-introduction is concise, relevant, and evidence-based. Organize your personal information, relevant experience, and strengths clearly. Add a tailored motivation statement after reviewing the job description, and aim for 2–3 minutes (approximately 200–300 English words).

Part 2

Master the Structured Interview

Understand → Structure → Identify → Match → Adapt → Apply

Step 1 • Understand

What Is a Structured Interview?

A structured interview uses job-related questions to assess candidates against specific competencies. Strong answers go beyond the question itself and provide evidence of what the interviewer is looking for. Even if an interviewer does not formally follow a structured interview approach, the core logic is similar: they want to understand whether you fit the role.

The key question to ask yourself:

“What is the interviewer really looking for behind this question?”

Step 2 • Structure

Use the STAR Framework

S

Situation

Set the context.

T

Task

Explain your responsibility or challenge.

A

Action

Explain specifically what you did, how, and why.

R

Result

Show the outcome, impact, feedback, or learning.

Tip: Spend more time on Action and Result.
Step 3 • Check

Quick Check: Think Like an Interviewer

“Tell me about a time you handled a difficult stakeholder.”

What is the interviewer most likely assessing?

Step 4 • Case Sharing Principle

Prepare Experiences, Not Answers

Interview questions may look different, but many assess similar underlying qualities. Instead of memorizing one answer for every possible question, identify what the interviewer wants to understand and select an experience that provides relevant evidence.

The Essence

One strong experience can answer multiple interview questions — but the emphasis should change according to what the interviewer is looking for.

① QuestionWhat are they asking?
② IntentionWhat are they looking for?
③ ExperienceWhich case proves it?
④STARHow will I organize it?
⑤AdaptWhat should I emphasize?

Step 7 • Apply

Prepare One Versatile Case Story

Choose one strong experience that can demonstrate more than one competency. Structure it using STAR, then think about how you could adapt it to different interview questions.

Tips for a strong STAR answer
  • Make clear which competency your example demonstrates.
  • Follow the STAR structure with specific, relevant details.
  • Emphasize your own actions, not only the team's work.
  • Include a concrete result, impact, or learning.
  • Consider how to adapt the same case to different questions.

Self-Evaluation: Six Dimensions

For each dimension, decide whether your case meets the criterion. Choose Complete if it does, or Needs Work if you still need to revise it. A revision box will appear only when you select Needs Work.

1. Competency Alignment

Does the case directly answer the interview question and show the intended competency?

2. STAR Structure

Can the interviewer identify the Situation, Task, Action, and Result?

3. Specific & Relevant Details

Have you included concrete examples, scope, context, or evidence?

4. Personal Actions

Is it clear what you personally did, how you did it, and why?

5. Results & Learning

Are the outcomes, impact, feedback, or lessons clear?

6. Adaptability

Could you emphasize different aspects of this same case for other questions?

Mark all six dimensions to finish the self-evaluation.
Step 9 • Ask & Engage

Questions to Ask Your Interviewer

An interview is a two-way conversation. When the interviewer asks, “Do you have any questions for us?”, use the opportunity to understand the role, demonstrate genuine preparation, and decide whether the opportunity is right for you.

?
Good questions create a conversation—not another interview.

Prepare 3–5 thoughtful questions in advance, then choose 2–3 that have not already been answered. Listen carefully and ask a relevant follow-up when appropriate.

Four principles for asking strong questions

01
Make it role-specific

Connect your question to the job description, responsibilities, or team rather than asking something generic.

02
Show curiosity, not assumptions

Use open-ended, neutral wording. Invite the interviewer to share their perspective.

03
Focus on contribution and fit

Explore expectations, success measures, collaboration, and development.

04
Prioritize and time it well

Avoid questions already answered. Save detailed pay or benefit negotiations for the appropriate stage.

Recommended questions by purpose

Use these as examples, not a script. Select a category to explore questions and why they are useful.

Rephrase rather than avoid difficult topics.
✕ LESS EFFECTIVE

“How soon can I get promoted?”

✓ MORE EFFECTIVE

“What opportunities are there to develop new skills and take on greater responsibility?”

YOUR TURN

Prepare your questions

Prepare two thoughtful questions for your interviewer, then post them on the Padlet board below. For example, you could ask about the role or team, or about growth opportunities and next steps.

Possible question topics:
  • About the role or team
  • About growth or next steps

These are examples only. Choose questions relevant to the position you're applying for.

Part 2 Key Takeaway

Strong interview preparation is not about memorizing perfect answers. Build relevant experiences, understand what the interviewer is looking for, structure evidence with STAR, adapt your emphasis to the question, and ask thoughtful questions that help you assess the opportunity.

Professional Interview Etiquette

Dress Code → Match the Scenario → Before / During / After → Practice

Step 1 • Dress Code

Choose an Appropriate Interview Outfit

Dress expectations vary by industry, role and employer. Choose clean, comfortable, well-fitting clothes that match the organization's professional environment. The examples below show options for both men and women; learners can choose any appropriate style.

Tip: When unsure, choose business casual or slightly more formal clothing. Keep shoes clean, accessories unobtrusive and your appearance neat.

Step 4 • Apply

Your Interview Journey: Before, During & After

1
BEFORE

Prepare with purpose

Know the role, plan your examples, and check the interview details.

Research the employer and rolePrepare STAR examples and questionsConfirm time, venue or meeting link, and outfit
2
DURING

Communicate with confidence

Show respect, listen attentively, and make your answers easy to follow.

Listen without interruptingUse relevant examples and clear structureMaintain professional body language
3
AFTER

Close the loop professionally

Follow up thoughtfully and use the experience to improve your next interview.

✉
Send a thank-you

Where appropriate, send a brief message within 24–48 hours. Thank the interviewer and reaffirm your interest.

✎
Reflect & improve

Note the questions asked, identify strengths and gaps, and refine your STAR stories.

↗
Follow up politely

Respect the stated timeline. If it passes, send one concise and courteous follow-up.

Part 3 • Key Takeaway

Professionalism Before, During, and After

Dress appropriately for the organization and role, communicate respectfully throughout the interview, and follow up thoughtfully afterward. Professional interview etiquette is not only about appearance—it is about preparation, attentiveness, and leaving a positive impression.
